stem: A 27-year-old woman has 4 days of right eye pain that worsens with eye movement, blurred vision, and washed-out color vision. On the swinging-flashlight test, both pupils constrict less when light is shone in her right eye than when it is shone in her left eye. Which structure is dysfunctional?

options.text: Right oculomotor cranial nerve pathway
Right optic sensory cranial nerve trunk
Left optic sensory cranial nerve trunk
Right Edinger-Westphal visceral nucleus
Central decussating optic chiasm tract

explanation: Right optic nerve. A relative afferent pupillary defect (Marcus Gunn pupil) means the afferent limb is impaired: light in the affected eye drives weaker constriction in both eyes. A CN III lesion would instead leave the right pupil large and unreactive to light in either eye. Optic neuritis is a common first presentation of MS.

stem: A 27-year-old woman presents with acute right optic neuritis and visual blurring. Brain MRI demonstrates ovoid T2-hyperintense demyelinating lesions oriented perpendicularly to the lateral ventricles (Dawson fingers). Which cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) finding best supports the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Elevated CSF protein with normal leukocyte count
Persistent xanthochromia with non-clearing RBCs
Intrathecal oligoclonal bands on electrophoresis
Marked neutrophilic pleocytosis with low glucose
Elevated 14-3-3 protein and tau on CSF analysis

explanation: Oligoclonal IgG bands (with raised IgG index and myelin basic protein) reflect intrathecal antibody synthesis in MS. Albuminocytologic dissociation is Guillain-Barré; xanthochromia suggests subarachnoid hemorrhage; 14-3-3 suggests CJD.

stem: A 27-year-old woman with multiple sclerosis presenting with acute optic neuritis and periventricular white matter lesions undergoes biopsy of an active demyelinating plaque. Which histological feature is most characteristically observed?

options.text: Axonal transection with preserved surrounding myelin sheath layers
Spongiform vacuolation and widespread neuronal loss without pus
Neutrophil-rich liquefactive necrosis containing bacterial rods
Perivascular mononuclear cuffs with demyelination and axonal sparing
Pseudopalisading necrosis surrounded by microvascular capillaries

explanation: MS plaques show myelin loss with relatively preserved axons, perivascular lymphocyte and macrophage cuffs, and later gliosis. Pseudopalisading necrosis is glioblastoma.

stem: A 24-year-old woman has horizontal double vision. On looking left, her right eye does not adduct while her left eye abducts with nystagmus; convergence is normal. Which lesion best explains this?

options.text: Left abducens somatic motor nucleus
Left medial longitudinal fasciculus
Right oculomotor somatic motor core
Right paramedian pontine reticular
Right medial longitudinal fasciculus

explanation: Internuclear ophthalmoplegia is named for the side of the adduction failure, which is the side of the MLF lesion. Left gaze uses the left abducens nucleus, whose internuclear neurons cross to the right MLF to reach the right medial rectus subnucleus. Convergence is spared because the oculomotor nucleus is intact. Bilateral INO in a young adult suggests MS.

stem: A 33-year-old woman with multiple sclerosis feels an electric shock down her spine on neck flexion, and her vision blurs transiently after a hot shower. What best explains the heat-induced worsening?

options.text: Conduction block in demyelinated central axons from rising core heat
Heat-induced transient ischemic vasospasm of small pial vasa nervorum
Formation of a new acute active inflammatory demyelinating brain lesion
Thermal activation of circulating serum complement and cytokine cascades
Acute elevation of intracranial cerebrospinal fluid opening pressure wave

explanation: Uhthoff phenomenon: warming worsens conduction through demyelinated axons (conduction block) without a new lesion. Lhermitte sign reflects cervical dorsal column demyelination.

stem: A 29-year-old woman with relapsing-remitting MS has 4 days of new left leg weakness; MRI shows a new enhancing lesion. What is the best treatment of this acute relapse?

options.text: Subcutaneous recombinant interferon-beta
Intravenous pooled human immunoglobulin
High-dose intravenous methylprednisolone
Subcutaneous synthetic glatiramer acetate
Conservative outpatient clinical observation

explanation: High-dose IV methylprednisolone shortens relapses. Interferon-β and glatiramer acetate are disease-modifying therapies, not relapse treatment. Plasma exchange is second-line for steroid-refractory relapses.

stem: A 45-year-old man was diagnosed with relapsing-remitting MS at age 28. Over the past 3 years his gait has worsened steadily without distinct relapses or new enhancing lesions. Which course does he now have?

options.text: Clinically isolated demyelinating syndrome
Relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis form
Primary progressive multiple sclerosis form
Secondary progressive multiple sclerosis form
Acute disseminated encephalomyelitis disease

explanation: Steady progression without relapses after years of relapsing-remitting disease (typically more than 10 years) is secondary progressive MS. Primary progressive MS is progressive from onset.

stem: A 36-year-old woman develops bilateral optic neuritis, then severe paraparesis 4 days later. Spinal MRI shows one T2-hyperintense lesion spanning five vertebral segments; brain MRI is normal. Which autoantibody is most likely?

options.text: Anti-acetylcholine receptor autoantibody
Anti-GQ1b ganglioside surface autoantibody
Anti-glutamic acid decarboxylase antibody
Anti-NMDA receptor glutamate autoantibody
Anti-aquaporin-4 water channel autoantibody

explanation: NMO spectrum disorder: anti-aquaporin-4 IgG against astrocyte foot processes; optic neuritis plus longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis (3 or more segments); brain MRI often normal. Acute treatment is steroids or plasma exchange; long-term azathioprine, mycophenolate, rituximab, or eculizumab. Interferon-β can worsen NMO.

stem: A 33-year-old man has leg weakness ascending over several days, tingling, and absent patellar and ankle reflexes. He had diarrhea after eating undercooked chicken 4 weeks ago. Which CSF finding is expected?

options.text: Neutrophilic pleocytosis with marked low glucose
Albuminocytologic dissociation on spinal fluid
Intrathecal oligoclonal bands with normal protein
Lymphocytic pleocytosis with normal glucose level
Persistent xanthochromia with crenated red cells

explanation: Elevated protein with normal cell count (albuminocytologic dissociation) is classic for GBS (AIDP), which follows Campylobacter jejuni through molecular mimicry between bacterial and Schwann cell/myelin epitopes.

stem: A 32-year-old man presents with progressive, symmetric ascending lower extremity weakness and diffuse hyporeflexia 2 weeks after an episode of diarrheal illness. Lumbar puncture demonstrates albuminocytologic dissociation with elevated CSF protein and normal cell count, confirming Guillain-Barré syndrome. Which monitoring measure is most critical to guide ongoing inpatient management?

options.text: Serial forced vital capacity and negative inspiratory force
Serial neuroimaging with contrast-enhanced spinal spinal MRI
Continuous video electroencephalographic seizure monitoring
Serial monitoring of serum creatine kinase enzyme levels
Serial daily diagnostic therapeutic lumbar spinal punctures

explanation: Respiratory muscle weakness can cause respiratory failure, so follow FVC and NIF. Treat with IVIG or plasma exchange; steroids are not indicated. Also monitor for dysautonomia.

stem: Why do most patients with Guillain-Barré syndrome recover better than patients with MS?

options.text: Peripheral somatic motor and sensory axons are never injured
Peripheral nerve myelin sheaths lack immunogenic antigens
Systemic corticosteroid therapy produces definitive remissions
Schwann cells readily proliferate and remyelinate axons in PNS
Single Schwann cells reliably myelinate multiple axonal fibers

explanation: Schwann cells proliferate and remyelinate; CNS oligodendrocytes do not remyelinate effectively, so MS lesions leave lasting deficits. Each Schwann cell myelinates one segment of a single axon.

stem: A 10-year-old girl has burning leg pain, clumsiness, pes cavus, hammer toes, distal leg atrophy, steppage gait, reduced vibration sense below the ankles, and slowed peroneal nerve conduction velocity. Which genetic abnormality is most likely?

options.text: PMP22 gene duplication on chromosome 17p
GAA trinucleotide repeat expansion in FXN
Dystrophin gene deletion on chromosome Xp
CAG trinucleotide expansion in huntingtin
SMN1 exon deletion on locus chromosome 5q

explanation: CMT1A: PMP22 duplication (chromosome 17), an autosomal dominant demyelinating neuropathy with slowed conduction velocity, distal atrophy, pes cavus, and hammer toes. Friedreich ataxia is a GAA repeat in FXN.

stem: A 48-year-old man with alcohol use disorder is admitted with a serum sodium of 108 mEq/L and receives hypertonic saline; sodium reaches 124 mEq/L within 24 hours. Three days later he is quadriparetic, dysarthric, and dysphagic but alert, with preserved vertical eye movements. What is the diagnosis?

options.text: Wernicke encephalopathy from severe thiamine depletion
Acute vasogenic cerebral edema from rapid rehydration
Osmotic demyelination syndrome of the central pontine
Progressive multifocal leukopathy from viral infection
Basilar artery thrombosis producing ventral brainstem loss

explanation: Osmotic demyelination (central pontine myelinolysis) follows overly rapid correction of chronic hyponatremia; corticospinal and corticobulbar involvement causes quadriparesis and pseudobulbar signs with preserved vertical gaze (locked-in picture). Alcohol use and malnutrition raise the risk.

stem: A 7-year-old boy develops fever, confusion, ataxia, and bilateral visual loss 2 weeks after an upper respiratory infection. MRI shows multifocal, large, asymmetric T2 lesions in white matter and deep gray matter. He has had no prior episodes. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis form
Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy
Herpes simplex virus necrotizing encephalitis
Neuromyelitis optica spectrum demyelination
Acute disseminated encephalomyelitis disease

explanation: ADEM: monophasic post-infectious or post-vaccine perivenular demyelination in children, with encephalopathy and multifocal deficits; treat with high-dose steroids. MS and NMO relapse over time.

stem: Which statement about myelin is correct?

options.text: Single oligodendrocytes myelinate segments of multiple central axons
Single Schwann cells myelinate segments of multiple peripheral axons
Astrocytic processes generate myelin sheaths within peripheral nerves
Central and peripheral myelin sheaths regenerate with equal velocity
Guillain-Barré syndrome selectively destroys central oligodendrocytes

explanation: One oligodendrocyte myelinates segments of multiple CNS axons, whereas one Schwann cell myelinates a single segment of one axon.

stem: A 62-year-old man has sudden severe unsteadiness: he cannot sit upright unsupported and has a wide-based gait, nystagmus, and vertigo. Finger-to-nose and heel-to-shin testing are normal. Which cerebellar division is infarcted?

options.text: Cerebrocerebellar lateral hemispheric zone
Spinocerebellar intermediate hemisphere zone
Vestibulocerebellar flocculonodular lobe zone
Deep cerebellar lateral dentate nuclear zone
Basilar pontine relay crossing pathway cells

explanation: Flocculonodular lobe (vestibulocerebellum): vertigo, nystagmus, and truncal instability with preserved limb coordination. It connects with the vestibular nuclei through the inferior cerebellar peduncle.

stem: A 45-year-old woman cannot control her left arm: it shakes as she brings a fork to her mouth, she overshoots, rapid hand flipping is clumsy, and speech is slurred. Strength and sensation are normal. Where is the lesion?

options.text: Right cerebellar hemisphere mass
Left cerebellar vermis midline zone
Right primary motor cortex precentral
Left cerebellar hemisphere pathology
Left basal ganglia striatum lesion

explanation: Cerebellar hemispheric lesions cause ipsilateral limb ataxia (intention tremor, dysmetria, dysdiadochokinesia, scanning dysarthria). The circuit crosses twice (corticopontocerebellar, then dentatothalamic via the superior cerebellar peduncle) and the corticospinal tract crosses again, so deficits are ipsilateral.

stem: A tumor compresses the main efferent pathway of the dentate nucleus as it leaves the cerebellum, causing ipsilateral intention tremor and dysmetria. Which structure is compressed?

options.text: Inferior cerebellar peduncle tract
Superior cerebellar peduncle tract
Middle cerebellar peduncle pathway
Flocculonodular vestibular nuclei
Interposed fastigial nuclear core

explanation: Dentate output leaves through the superior cerebellar peduncle, decussates, and ascends to the contralateral VL thalamus and red nucleus.

stem: Which cell is the sole output neuron of the cerebellar cortex, and what is its neurotransmitter?

options.text: Granule cell; glutamate transmitter
Purkinje cell; GABA neurotransmitter
Golgi neuron; glycine neurotransmitter
Basket cell; glutamate neurotransmitter
Climbing fiber; GABA neurotransmitter

explanation: Purkinje cells are the only output of the cerebellar cortex and are inhibitory (GABA) onto deep nuclei. Mossy fibers excite them via granule cells and parallel fibers; climbing fibers from the inferior olive excite them directly.

stem: A 65-year-old woman with 15 years of heavy alcohol use has 5 months of progressive gait disturbance. She has a wide-based gait, cannot tandem walk, and sways side to side when seated. Finger-to-nose and heel-to-shin tests are normal; vibration and proprioception are intact; no nystagmus. Which structure is most affected?

options.text: Lateral cerebellar hemispheres
Caudal flocculonodular lobe core
Ascending dorsal funiculus columns
Deep cerebellar lateral dentates
Anterior rostral cerebellar vermis

explanation: Alcohol-related degeneration of the anterior (rostral) vermis (spinocerebellum) produces truncal and gait ataxia with normal limb testing.

stem: A 55-year-old man has 6 months of unsteady wide-based gait, lancinating leg pain, and urinary retention. Vibration and proprioception are impaired in the feet, Romberg is positive, ankle reflexes are absent, and his pupils accommodate but do not react to light. Heel-to-shin and rapid alternating movements are normal. What is the diagnosis and treatment?

options.text: Friedreich ataxia; compassionate supportive therapy
Cobalamin B12 deficiency; intramuscular cyanocobalamin
Tabes dorsalis neurosyphilis; intravenous penicillin G
Alcoholic vermian degeneration; intravenous thiamine
Multiple sclerosis relapse; intravenous methylprednisolone

explanation: Tabes dorsalis: dorsal column and dorsal root damage from tertiary syphilis (sensory ataxia, positive Romberg, lancinating pain, absent reflexes, Argyll Robertson pupils). Treat with IV penicillin G. B12 deficiency can cause posterior column signs but not Argyll Robertson pupils.

stem: A 66-year-old woman has brief episodes of vertigo when turning her head to the left. Placing her head back with the left ear down reproduces rotatory nystagmus and nausea. Hearing is normal. What is the best next step?

options.text: Canalith repositioning Epley maneuver
Contrast-enhanced cranial brain MRI
High-dose intravenous methylprednisolone
Urgent diagnostic lumbar spinal puncture
Formal comprehensive audiometric testing

explanation: BPPV: otoliths displaced into the posterior semicircular canal. Dix-Hallpike diagnoses it; the Epley maneuver treats it.

stem: A 14-year-old boy has progressive gait ataxia, scoliosis, pes cavus, absent deep tendon reflexes, impaired vibration and proprioception, and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. What is the underlying mechanism?

options.text: Unstable CAG trinucleotide expansion in the ataxin-1 gene locus
Peripheral myelin protein 22 duplication on human chromosome 17p
Mutations in ATP7B producing pathological systemic copper storage
Unstable GAA repeat in FXN causing mitochondrial iron overload
In-frame deletion of dystrophin on short arm of the X chromosome

explanation: Friedreich ataxia: autosomal recessive GAA expansion in FXN causes frataxin deficiency, mitochondrial iron accumulation, and oxidative injury of dorsal columns, spinocerebellar tracts, and heart. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is the usual cause of death.

stem: A 62-year-old man has sudden vertigo, hoarseness, left Horner syndrome, left-sided limb ataxia, and loss of pain and temperature on the left face and right body. Which structure explains his left limb ataxia?

options.text: Inferior cerebellar peduncle pathway
Superior cerebellar peduncle pathway
Middle cerebellar peduncle input tract
Ascending medial lemniscal sensory core
Descending medullary pyramidal motor core

explanation: In Wallenberg syndrome, damage to the inferior cerebellar peduncle (dorsal spinocerebellar and olivocerebellar fibers) causes ipsilateral limb ataxia.

stem: A lesion interrupts unconscious proprioceptive information from the right leg to the cerebellum. Which pathway is affected?

options.text: Left lateral corticospinal tract descending to the spinal cord
Left dorsal spinocerebellar tract entering the inferior peduncle
Ipsilateral fasciculus gracilis tract ascending to caudal medulla
Contralateral medial lemniscus tract ascending to the VPL nucleus
Right dorsal spinocerebellar tract entering the inferior peduncle

explanation: Unconscious proprioception from the leg travels ipsilaterally in the dorsal spinocerebellar tract through the inferior cerebellar peduncle. Conscious proprioception travels in the dorsal columns and medial lemniscus.

stem: A 55-year-old man with atrial fibrillation has a cerebellar infarct with vertigo, vomiting, gait ataxia, and headache. On day 3 he becomes drowsy; CT shows cerebellar swelling compressing the fourth ventricle with hydrocephalus. What is the most urgent intervention?

options.text: Therapeutic lumbar puncture to decrease intracranial pressure
Intravenous tissue plasminogen activator thrombolytic infusion
High-dose oral aspirin antiplatelet therapy without thrombolysis
Aggressive antihypertensive therapy lowering mean arterial pressure
Neurosurgical suboccipital decompressive craniectomy surgery

explanation: Cerebellar infarct edema peaks around days 2–4 and can compress the fourth ventricle and brainstem. Treat with suboccipital decompression (with or without EVD). Lumbar puncture risks herniation.

stem: The flocculonodular lobe projects directly to which structure?

options.text: Deep lateral cerebellar dentate nucleus
Intermediate cerebellar emboliform core
Rostral midbrain tegmental red nucleus
Brainstem vestibular nuclear complexes
Thalamic ventral lateral relay nucleus

explanation: The flocculonodular lobe projects directly to the vestibular nuclei (and via the fastigial nucleus), controlling balance and the vestibulo-ocular reflex.

stem: A 58-year-old man has a first generalized seizure. MRI shows a heterogeneous ring-enhancing mass with central necrosis crossing the corpus callosum. What is the expected histology?

options.text: Whorled spindle cells with concentric calcified psammoma bodies
Perivascular pseudorosettes surrounding central hyalinized vessels
Fried-egg cells with round nuclei and chicken-wire capillaries
Pseudopalisading necrosis surrounded by microvascular proliferation
Small round blue cells arranged in classic Homer Wright rosettes

explanation: Glioblastoma: pseudopalisading necrosis and microvascular proliferation, GFAP positive, butterfly pattern across the corpus callosum, EGFR amplification.

stem: A 29-year-old man has a seizure; imaging shows a calcified frontal mass. Biopsy shows round cells with perinuclear halos and a delicate branching capillary network. Which genetic alteration is expected?

options.text: Oligodendroglioma showing 1p/19q codeletion
Pilocytic astrocytoma with Rosenthal fibers
Glioblastoma with pseudopalisading necrosis
Medulloblastoma showing Homer Wright rosettes
Meningioma showing whorled psammoma bodies

explanation: Oligodendroglioma: fried-egg cells, chicken-wire capillaries, calcification, 1p/19q codeletion (better prognosis, chemosensitive).

stem: A 60-year-old woman has 2 months of personality change and headache. MRI shows an extra-axial, dural-based, homogeneously enhancing mass with a dural tail. What does the resected specimen show?

options.text: Whorls of spindle cells with psammoma bodies
Rosenthal fibers with eosinophilic bodies
Sheets of small round hyperchromatic cells
Compact Antoni A cellular palisading zones
Lipid-laden stromal cells with capillaries

explanation: Meningioma: arachnoid cap cell tumor with whorled spindle cells, psammoma bodies, and a dural tail; more common in women and ER/PR positive. Slow growth explains late symptoms.

stem: A 45-year-old woman has progressive left hearing loss, tinnitus, and imbalance. MRI shows an enhancing mass in the left cerebellopontine angle extending into the internal auditory canal. Which histologic features are expected?

options.text: Whorled meningothelial cell nests and calcified psammoma bodies
Biphasic compact cellular Antoni A and myxoid Antoni B regions
Fried-egg clear cytoplasm cells surrounded by chicken-wire beds
Homer Wright neuroblastic pseudorosettes of small blue cells
Perivascular pseudo-rosettes with tapering fibrillary processes

explanation: Vestibular schwannoma: S-100 positive Schwann cell tumor with dense Antoni A areas (Verocay bodies) and loose Antoni B areas.

stem: A 17-year-old boy has bilateral sensorineural hearing loss, bilateral cerebellopontine angle masses, two meningiomas, and posterior subcapsular cataracts. His father is similarly affected. Which gene product is deficient?

options.text: Neurofibromin tumor suppressor on chromosome 17q
VHL tumor suppressor protein on chromosome 3p25
Hamartin tumor suppressor on chromosome 9q34
Merlin tumor suppressor protein on chromosome 22q
Tuberin tumor suppressor protein on chromosome 16p

explanation: NF2 (chromosome 22, merlin): bilateral vestibular schwannomas, meningiomas, ependymomas, and juvenile cataracts; autosomal dominant.

stem: An 8-year-old girl has café-au-lait macules, axillary freckling, iris Lisch nodules, and progressive painless vision loss in the left eye with a relative afferent pupillary defect. MRI shows optic nerve enlargement. What is the normal function of the deficient protein?

options.text: Links actin cytoskeleton to membrane proteins for contact inhibition
Targets hypoxia-inducible factor alpha for proteasomal degradation
Forms intracellular complexes with tuberin to inhibit mTOR signaling
Transduces cell-surface signals through G protein alpha-q pathways
Inactivates downstream Ras GTPases to negatively regulate cell growth

explanation: NF1 (chromosome 17): neurofibromin is a Ras GTPase-activating protein; loss increases Ras signaling. Features include optic glioma, Lisch nodules, café-au-lait macules, and neurofibromas.

stem: A 9-year-old boy has headache, vomiting, and ataxia. MRI shows a cystic cerebellar hemispheric mass with an enhancing mural nodule. What is the expected histology?

options.text: Small round blue cells with classic Homer Wright rosettes
Biphasic astrocytes with Rosenthal fibers and granular bodies
Necrotic pseudopalisades with microvascular proliferation
Alternating Antoni A and B cellular areas with Verocay bodies
Concentric whorled arachnoid cap cells with psammoma bodies

explanation: Pilocytic astrocytoma (WHO grade I): cystic with mural nodule, biphasic histology, Rosenthal fibers, eosinophilic granular bodies, GFAP positive, excellent prognosis.

stem: A 4-year-old boy has morning vomiting, headache, clumsy gait, and bilateral papilledema. MRI shows a midline vermian mass filling the fourth ventricle; biopsy shows small round blue cells forming rosettes. What is the diagnosis?

options.text: Cerebellar pilocytic astrocytoma
Fourth ventricle ependymoma tumor
Cerebellar vermis medulloblastoma
Suprasellar craniopharyngioma mass
Temporal lobe ganglioglioma tumor

explanation: Medulloblastoma: vermian small round blue cell tumor with Homer Wright rosettes, obstructive hydrocephalus from fourth ventricle compression, and drop metastases.

stem: A 2-year-old boy has daily vomiting, bilateral papilledema, and a wide-based gait with normal finger-to-nose testing. What is the best next step?

options.text: Lumbar puncture to assess opening pressure
Immediate empiric intravenous ceftriaxone
Routine outpatient electroencephalography
Parental reassurance without intervention
Brain neuroimaging before lumbar puncture

explanation: Papilledema indicates raised ICP; image first. Lumbar puncture risks tonsillar herniation.

stem: A 6-year-old girl has headache, vomiting, and head tilt. MRI shows a mass arising from the floor of the fourth ventricle extending through the foramina of Luschka and Magendie. What is the characteristic histologic feature?

options.text: Perivascular pseudorosettes in fourth ventricle floor
Homer Wright neuroblastic rosettes in vermis tumor
Eosinophilic Rosenthal fibers in cerebellar astrocytoma
Cellular Verocay bodies within cerebellopontine angle
Laminated psammoma bodies in parasagittal meningioma

explanation: Ependymoma: fourth ventricle floor in children, with perivascular pseudorosettes. Homer Wright rosettes point to medulloblastoma.

stem: A 10-year-old boy has bitemporal hemianopia and short stature. MRI shows a calcified, cystic suprasellar mass. From what tissue does this tumor arise?

options.text: Arachnoid cap cells of the dura mater layer
Embryonic Rathke pouch epithelial remnants
Posterior pituitary neurohypophyseal cells
Ependymal cells lining the third ventricle
External granular layer neuroblast cells

explanation: Craniopharyngioma arises from Rathke pouch remnants: calcified suprasellar cyst with motor-oil fluid, bitemporal hemianopia, growth failure.

stem: A 6-month-old has infantile spasms and hypopigmented ash-leaf macules. Echocardiography shows a cardiac rhabdomyoma; MRI shows subependymal nodules. What is the underlying molecular defect?

options.text: Biallelic loss of NF1 neurofibromin
Biallelic loss of VHL tumor protein
Inactivating mutations in TSC1 or TSC2
Activating mosaic mutations in GNAQ
Biallelic loss of NF2 merlin protein

explanation: Tuberous sclerosis: TSC1 (hamartin, chromosome 9) or TSC2 (tuberin, chromosome 16) loss activates mTOR. Cortical tubers, subependymal giant cell astrocytoma, ash-leaf macules, cardiac rhabdomyoma.

stem: A 20-year-old woman with epilepsy since childhood has facial angiofibromas, a leathery orange-peel patch on the lower back, periungual fibromas, hematuria, and bilateral flank masses of fat density on CT. What is the renal lesion?

options.text: Clear cell renal cell carcinoma
Pediatric nephroblastoma tumor
Benign renal oncocytoma neoplasm
Renal angiomyolipoma with fat
Urothelial transitional carcinoma

explanation: Renal angiomyolipoma (fat density) is typical of tuberous sclerosis, along with shagreen patch, angiofibromas, and ungual fibromas.

stem: A newborn has a unilateral port-wine stain of the forehead and upper eyelid, seizures, and glaucoma. Which neuroimaging finding is expected?

options.text: Bilateral cerebellopontine angle acoustic schwannoma masses
Cerebellar capillary hemangioblastoma with cystic nodules
Optic nerve juvenile pilocytic astrocytoma with proptosis
Subependymal giant cell astrocytomas lining ventricles
Ipsilateral leptomeningeal angioma with cortical tracks

explanation: Sturge-Weber: mosaic GNAQ mutation, V1 port-wine stain, leptomeningeal angioma, tram-track gyral calcifications, glaucoma, and seizures.

stem: A 30-year-old man has a cerebellar hemangioblastoma and retinal angiomas; his father had renal cancer. Which additional tumors is he at risk for?

options.text: Dural meningiomas and acoustic vestibular schwannomas
Clear cell renal cell carcinoma and pheochromocytoma
Optic pathway gliomas and cutaneous neurofibroma foci
Cardiac rhabdomyomas and bilateral angiomyolipomas
Leptomeningeal facial angiomas and secondary glaucoma

explanation: Von Hippel-Lindau (VHL, chromosome 3p): loss stabilizes HIF and raises VEGF. Hemangioblastomas, clear cell renal cell carcinoma, and pheochromocytoma.

stem: A 62-year-old smoker has multiple ring-enhancing lesions at the gray-white junction with vasogenic edema. What is the most likely primary site?

options.text: Prostate adenocarcinoma carcinoma
Primary bronchogenic lung carcinoma
Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma
Follicular thyroid adenocarcinoma
Esophageal squamous adenocarcinoma

explanation: Metastases are the most common adult brain tumors, at the gray-white junction; lung is the most frequent primary (then breast, melanoma, kidney, colon).

stem: An 8-year-old boy has temporal lobe seizures. A cortical cystic, calcified lesion contains neoplastic binucleated ganglion cells with a glial component. What is the diagnosis?

options.text: Ganglioglioma with dysplastic neurons
Oligodendroglioma with fried-egg cells
Transitional meningioma with whorls
Medulloblastoma with Homer Wrights
Ependymoma with true ependymal rings

explanation: Ganglioglioma: neoplastic ganglion cells with glial component, children and young adults, temporal lobe seizures.

stem: A 55-year-old man with a large frontal glioblastoma becomes lethargic with an ipsilateral dilated, nonreactive pupil and contralateral hemiparesis. What is the mechanism?

options.text: Subfalcine herniation with compression of anterior cerebral artery
Tonsillar herniation with compression of lower medullary centers
Upward transtentorial herniation with compression of midbrain
Uncal herniation with compression of ipsilateral oculomotor nerve
Foramen magnum impaction with compression of glossopharyngeal core

explanation: Uncal herniation compresses CN III (parasympathetic fibers cause the dilated pupil) and can compress the contralateral cerebral peduncle; Duret hemorrhages may follow.

stem: Which is the best agent to reduce peritumoral vasogenic edema?

options.text: Intravenous mannitol maintenance therapy
Oral acetazolamide carbonic anhydrase block
Prolonged mechanical hyperventilation therapy
Loop diuretic therapy with oral furosemide
Systemic corticosteroid with dexamethasone

explanation: Dexamethasone reduces vasogenic peritumoral edema by stabilizing the blood-brain barrier.

stem: Which histologic feature distinguishes glioblastoma (WHO grade IV) from anaplastic astrocytoma (grade III)?

options.text: Nuclear cellular atypia
Marked hypercellularity
Necrosis and vascularity
Positive GFAP reactivity
Elevated mitotic figure

explanation: Glioblastoma (grade IV) shows necrosis and/or microvascular proliferation; anaplastic astrocytoma (grade III) does not.

stem: Which neurocutaneous syndrome is caused by a postzygotic somatic mutation and is not inherited?

options.text: Sturge-Weber mosaic syndrome
Neurofibromatosis type 1 disease
Neurofibromatosis type 2 disease
Von Hippel-Lindau genetic disease
Tuberous sclerosis complex disease

explanation: Sturge-Weber is sporadic (somatic mosaic GNAQ mutation); NF1, NF2, tuberous sclerosis, and VHL are inherited.

stem: A 22-year-old college freshman has fever, headache, neck stiffness, and a petechial rash. CSF shows opening pressure 35 cm H2O, 3,200 WBC/µL (90% neutrophils), protein 260 mg/dL, and glucose 18 mg/dL. Which organism is most likely?

options.text: Neisseria meningitidis diplococci
Listeria monocytogenes bacillus
Enterovirus viral meningoform
Cryptococcus neoformans yeast
Group B Streptococcus bacteria

explanation: Neisseria meningitidis is the leading cause of bacterial meningitis in young adults living in close quarters (college dorms) and is characteristically associated with a petechial/purpuric rash. CSF demonstrates marked neutrophilic pleocytosis, markedly elevated protein, and low glucose.

stem: A 72-year-old man on chemotherapy develops meningitis; CSF Gram stain shows gram-positive rods that tumble in culture. Which organism is responsible and what must be added to empiric therapy?

options.text: Neisseria meningitidis; rifampin prophylaxis
Streptococcus pneumoniae; vancomycin therapy
Haemophilus influenzae; ceftriaxone regimen
Listeria monocytogenes; ampicillin regimen
Cryptococcus neoformans; amphotericin B drip

explanation: Listeria monocytogenes is a facultative intracellular gram-positive rod with characteristic tumbling motility that causes meningitis in immunocompromised patients, neonates, and older adults (>50 years). Ampicillin must be added empirically because Listeria is intrinsically resistant to all cephalosporins.

stem: A 63-year-old man has fever of 40°C, confusion, word-finding difficulty, and vesicles on the upper lip. CSF shows lymphocytes and red blood cells; imaging is pending. What is the best next step?

options.text: Await confirmatory CSF HSV PCR prior to initiating therapy
Initiate intravenous ganciclovir therapy for cytomegalovirus
Initiate prompt intravenous acyclovir therapy immediately now
Initiate high-dose oral valacyclovir maintenance out-of-hospital
Initiate high-dose intravenous corticosteroid monotherapy now

explanation: Herpes simplex virus (HSV-1) encephalitis is a neurological emergency presenting with fever, altered mental status, and frontotemporal deficits. Hypoxemia-mediated vasodilation increasing cerebral blood perfusion
Enhanced arachnoid granulation uptake promoting cerebrospinal drain
Direct metabolic suppression slowing cortical bioelectric discharge
Rapid hyperosmolar fluid extraction across tight capillary barriers

Thalamic ventral posterolateral relay nucleus
Cerebellar vermis and flocculonodular cortex
Spinal cord cervical dorsal horn gray column
Rostral medulla and caudal pontine tegmentum

explanation: Cold-water caloric irrigation of the external auditory canal stimulates the vestibulo-ocular reflex (VOR). Right lateral pons territory; anterior inferior cerebellar
Right medial midbrain crus; posterior cerebral artery
Right medial medulla territory; anterior spinal artery
Left medial midbrain crus; paramedian basilar branches

explanation: Weber syndrome is an alternating hemiplegia caused by infarction of the ventromedial rostral midbrain (PCA paramedian branches). It interrupts the emerging CN III fascicles (producing ipsilateral third nerve palsy: ptosis, mydriasis, eye turned "down and out") and the crus cerebri / corticospinal tract (producing contralateral spastic hemiparesis).

She has loss of touch on the left body, loss of touch and pinprick on the left face, and left-sided intention tremor and dysmetria; strength is normal. Which structure explains the left limb ataxia?

Right superior cerebellar peduncle dentatorubrothalamic
Left middle cerebellar peduncle pontocerebellar pathway
Right descending corticospinal motor projection pathway
Left rubrospinal tract descending tegmental projections

stem: A 68-year-old man with atrial fibrillation has sudden somnolence, vertical gaze palsy, abnormal pupils, bilateral visual loss, and visual hallucinations. Which vessel segment is occluded?

Bilateral vertebral arterial segments and post-PICA
Proximal basilar arterial trunk and anterior branches
Anterior spinal artery midline ventromedial territory
Distal rostral basilar apex bifurcation and branches

explanation: Occlusion of the rostral basilar artery ("top of the basilar" syndrome) compromises blood flow to the bilateral posterior cerebral and superior cerebellar arteries. Ischemia to the bilateral thalami and upper midbrain results in profound somnolence or coma, vertical gaze palsies (Parinaud syndrome), and pupillary abnormalities.

stem: A 64-year-old man has difficulty chewing; his jaw deviates to the left on opening. He has loss of light touch on the left face, loss of pain and temperature on the right body, left ptosis and miosis, and left limb ataxia. Which level and artery are involved?

Caudal lateral pons; anterior inferior cerebellar
Rostral lateral medulla; posterior inferior artery
Caudal medial medulla; anterior spinal artery branch

explanation: Mid-pontine lateral infarction (basilar circumferential branches) involves the trigeminal motor and principal sensory nuclei and the spinothalamic tract. Patients exhibit ipsilateral weakness of the muscles of mastication (jaw deviates toward the side of the lesion), ipsilateral facial hemianesthesia, and contralateral loss of pain and temperature on the body.

stem: A 61-year-old hypertensive man has horizontal diplopia: his left eye is turned medially and cannot abduct. He has right hemiparesis with a Babinski sign, a right lower face droop with the forehead spared, tongue deviation to the right, and loss of light touch on the right body. Which lesion is most likely?

Left lateral caudal pons; anterior inferior cerebellar
Right medial rostral midbrain; posterior cerebral
Left medial caudal pons; basilar paramedian branches
Left medial caudal medulla; anterior spinal branches

explanation: A caudal medial pontine stroke (Millard-Gubler / Foville variant, supplied by basilar paramedian branches) interrupts the exiting CN VI fascicles (producing ipsilateral lateral rectus palsy with inability to abduct the eye) and the descending corticospinal tract in the basis pontis (producing contralateral spastic hemiparesis).

stem: A 62-year-old man has sudden vertigo, nausea, and left hearing loss. The entire left face is paralyzed, including the forehead. He has loss of pain and temperature on the left face and right body, left Horner syndrome, and left limb ataxia. Which artery is occluded?

Basilar arterial apex perforators
Anterior spinal midline branches
Posterior cerebral arterial branches
Anterior inferior cerebellar artery

explanation: Lateral inferior pontine syndrome is caused by occlusion of the anterior inferior cerebellar artery (AICA). Key distinguishing features include ipsilateral peripheral seventh nerve palsy (complete hemifacial paralysis including the forehead), hearing loss and tinnitus (CN VIII / labyrinthine artery), limb ataxia (middle cerebellar peduncle), and Horner syndrome.

stem: A 57-year-old man has sudden vertigo, vomiting, hoarseness, and dysphagia. He falls to the left, with left Horner syndrome, loss of pain and temperature on the left face and right body, and normal strength. Which artery is occluded?

options.text: Left anterior inferior cerebellar artery
Left posterior cerebral artery branches
Left posterior inferior cerebellar artery
Basilar arterial paramedian perforators
Anterior spinal midline spinal branches

explanation: Lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome is caused by occlusion of the posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA) or vertebral artery. Manifestations include dysphagia and hoarseness (nucleus ambiguus / CN IX, X), vertigo and nystagmus (vestibular nuclei), ipsilateral facial pain/temp loss (spinal V), contralateral body pain/temp loss (spinothalamic tract), ipsilateral Horner syndrome, and limb ataxia.

stem: A 57-year-old man with a left lateral medullary (Wallenberg) stroke develops dysphagia, hoarseness, and loss of the gag reflex due to nucleus ambiguus ischemia. To which side does the uvula deviate on examination, and why?

options.text: Leftward deviation toward the ischemic side from hypoglossal nerve injury
Remains precisely at the anatomical midline with symmetrical palatal rise
Leftward deviation toward the lesion because the ipsilateral palate elevates
Rightward deviation toward the lesion caused by glossopharyngeal nerve palsy
Rightward deviation away from lesion due to ipsilateral vagus nerve weakness

explanation: In lateral medullary syndrome, ischemia of the nucleus ambiguus impairs motor innervation of the ipsilateral levator veli palatini (CN X). When the patient says "ah", the intact contralateral muscle lifts the palate normally, causing the uvula to deviate AWAY from the side of the lesion (to the right in a left-sided Wallenberg stroke).

stem: A 63-year-old woman has left tongue deviation with atrophy and fasciculations, right hemiparesis with a Babinski sign, and loss of vibration and proprioception on the right body. There is no vertigo, face droop, or Horner syndrome. Which artery is occluded?

options.text: Anterior spinal artery midline territory
Anterior inferior cerebellar artery branch
Posterior inferior cerebellar artery branch
Posterior cerebral artery cortical branch
Basilar arterial tip and rostral branches

explanation: Medial medullary (Dejerine) syndrome is caused by occlusion of the anterior spinal artery (ASA). It damages the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII: ipsilateral flaccid tongue paralysis with deviation toward the lesion), the pyramidal tract (contralateral hemiparesis), and the medial lemniscus (contralateral loss of vibration and joint position sense).

stem: A 68-year-old man with atrial fibrillation collapses and over hours is found to be awake and following commands with his eyes. He has no limb, face, jaw, or speech movement; he can blink and move his eyes vertically. What is the diagnosis and vessel?

options.text: Locked-in state from ventral pontine infarction; basilar artery
Persistent vegetative coma state; middle cerebral arteries
Coma secondary to bilateral thalamic infarcts; PCA vessels
Akinetic mutism state from medial frontal infarcts; ACAs
Guillain-Barre demyelinating polyradiculopathy neuropathy

explanation: Locked-in syndrome is caused by basilar artery occlusion producing bilateral infarction of the basis pontis (ventral pons). Bilateral corticospinal and corticobulbar tracts are interrupted, causing total quadriplegia and anarthria. Because the tegmentum, reticular activating system, and CN III/IV are spared, patients remain fully conscious and communicate via vertical eye movements and blinking.

stem: A 65-year-old man has a right lower face droop with the forehead spared and right arm weakness. Why is the forehead spared?

The frontalis muscle is supplied solely by the contralateral facial branch
Frontalis fibers receive direct somatic motor innervation from cervical roots
Upper facial motor subnuclei receive bilateral corticobulbar projections
Lower facial motor subnuclei receive bilateral corticobulbar projections

explanation: The motor neurons of the facial nucleus that innervate the upper face (forehead) receive bilateral corticobulbar projections from both cerebral hemispheres, whereas lower facial motor neurons receive only contralateral input. A unilateral upper motor neuron (corticobulbar) lesion produces weakness of the contralateral lower face with sparing of the forehead.

stem: A 69-year-old woman has sudden numbness of the left face and body (touch, pain, and temperature), with no weakness, cranial nerve palsy, ataxia, or cognitive or visual deficit. Weeks later she develops burning pain. What is the lesion?

options.text: Posterolateral thalamic relay nuclei; thalamogeniculate PCA
Subthalamic motor nucleus territory; posterior cerebral artery
Lateral geniculate relay nucleus; anterior choroidal branch
Ventral anterior motor relay nucleus; lenticulostriate vessel
Mediodorsal cognitive thalamic nucleus; anterior cerebral branch

explanation: Infarction of the sensory thalamic relay nuclei (ventral posterolateral [VPL] and ventral posteromedial [VPM] nuclei, supplied by thalamogeniculate branches of PCA) causes contralateral hemisensory loss. Weeks to months later, patients may develop severe, intractable neuropathic burning pain (Dejerine-Roussy thalamic pain syndrome).

stem: A 70-year-old diabetic man has sudden violent flinging movements of the left arm and leg. Which lesion is most likely?

Right striatal caudate nuclear head zone
Left putaminal and insular nuclear matrix
Left subthalamic motor regulatory nucleus
Bilateral substantia nigra pars compacta

explanation: Hemiballismus consists of sudden, violent, involuntary flinging movements of the contralateral limbs. It is caused by a lesion (typically ischemic or hemorrhagic) of the contralateral subthalamic nucleus, which normally provides excitatory glutamatergic drive to the globus pallidus internus to inhibit unwanted motor movements.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Rule: Stroke (Blood Supply, Cerebrovascular, Brainstem)

stem: Which brainstem lesion would not be expected to cause ipsilateral Horner syndrome?

options.text: Lateral medullary syndrome Wallenberg infarct
Medial medullary syndrome Dejerine infarction
Lateral inferior pontine syndrome AICA stroke
Extracranial internal carotid artery rupture
Apical thoracic lung mass Pancoast tumor mass

explanation: The descending first-order sympathetic pathway travels through the lateral brainstem (lateral midbrain, lateral pons, and lateral medulla). A medial medullary infarct affects medial structures (pyramid, hypoglossal nerve, medial lemniscus) and characteristically spares the lateral sympathetic tract, so it will not cause Horner syndrome.

stem: Which level–artery pairing is correct?

options.text: Rostral midbrain dorsal zone; posterior inferior cerebellar artery
Caudal lateral pons tegmentum; posterior cerebral artery branches
Lateral medullary tegmentum; basilar arterial paramedian trunk
Medial medullary pyramid; anterior inferior cerebellar artery
Lateral medullary retro-olivary region; posterior inferior artery

explanation: The vascular supply of the brainstem follows predictable territorial branches: the rostral midbrain is supplied by the posterior cerebral artery (PCA) and superior cerebellar artery (SCA); the pons is supplied by the basilar artery; the lateral medulla by PICA; and the medial medulla by the anterior spinal artery (ASA).
