stem: A 78-year-old retired engineer has a year of worsening memory, repeats questions, gets lost in his neighborhood, and has trouble dressing and balancing his checkbook. He becomes defensive when asked. Examination and metabolic workup are normal. Which structure shows earliest atrophy?

options.text: Primary motor and primary sensory cerebral neocortical convolutions
Basal ganglia striatum and substantia nigra dopaminergic pars core
Medial temporal lobe hippocampus and entorhinal cortex structures
Dorsolateral prefrontal cortex and rostral frontopolar gray matter
Occipital striate calcarine cortex and peristriate visual pathways

explanation: Alzheimer disease is the most common cause of neurodegenerative dementia. Pathology typically begins in the transentorhinal cortex and progresses into the entorhinal cortex and hippocampus, resulting in early prominent atrophy of the medial temporal lobes and insidious decline in episodic memory.

stem: A 52-year-old man with Down syndrome has progressive memory and personality decline. Autopsy shows abundant amyloid plaques. What explains his early plaque deposition?

options.text: Expansion of unstable polymorphic trinucleotide repeat tract on DNA
Trisomy twenty-one resulting in excessive amyloid precursor dosage
Point missense mutation within presenilin-one gene on chromosome 14
Point missense mutation within presenilin-two gene on chromosome 1
Inheritance of the apolipoprotein E epsilon four susceptibility allele

explanation: The gene encoding Amyloid Precursor Protein (APP) is located on chromosome 21. Individuals with Down syndrome (Trisomy 21) possess an extra copy of the APP gene (gene dosage effect), resulting in elevated production of amyloid-beta peptides and early-onset Alzheimer disease pathology by age 40 to 50.

stem: Which process best explains the extracellular plaques of Alzheimer disease?

options.text: Sequential cleavage of precursor by alpha-secretase then beta-secretase
Sequential cleavage of precursor by alpha-secretase then gamma-secretase
Solitary single-site endopeptidase cleavage by beta-secretase enzyme
Sequential cleavage of precursor by beta-secretase then gamma-secretase
Zinc metalloprotease degradation and endopeptidase neprilysin cleavage

explanation: Senile (neuritic) plaques in Alzheimer disease consist of extracellular aggregates of amyloid-beta (Aβ42). Aβ42 is generated by the sequential amyloidogenic cleavage of Amyloid Precursor Protein (APP), first by beta-secretase (BACE1) and subsequently by intramembrane gamma-secretase (presenilin complex).

stem: A 66-year-old woman with Alzheimer disease starts donepezil. What are its mechanism and a common adverse effect?

options.text: Uncompetitive antagonist of N-methyl-D-aspartate glutamate receptors
Reversible centrally active inhibitor of acetylcholinesterase enzymes
Selective agonist stimulation of central postsynaptic D2 receptors
Inhibitor of presynaptic serotonin and norepinephrine transporter pumps
Targeted small molecule inhibitor of transmembrane gamma-secretase

explanation: Donepezil is a centrally active, reversible acetylcholinesterase inhibitor that increases acetylcholine availability in the cerebral cortex. Enhancing parasympathetic and central cholinergic activity commonly leads to cholinergic side effects, including gastrointestinal distress (nausea, diarrhea), vivid dreams, and bradycardia.

stem: A 79-year-old woman with moderate Alzheimer disease on donepezil has memantine added. What is its mechanism?

options.text: Reversible inhibitor of acetylcholinesterase enzyme
Uncompetitive antagonist of NMDA glutamate receptor
Blocker of persistent voltage-gated sodium channels
Allosteric modulator of post-junctional GABA-A pore
Competitive antagonist of central dopamine D2 sites

explanation: Memantine is an uncompetitive, moderate-affinity NMDA receptor antagonist. Pathological chronic mild elevation of extracellular glutamate leads to sustained calcium influx and excitotoxic neuronal death; memantine blocks this tonic pathological activation while preserving normal physiological synaptic transmission.

stem: A 64-year-old man punches in his sleep, sees children in the room who are not there, has fluctuating alertness, and mild parkinsonism; memory is relatively preserved. What histologic finding is expected?

options.text: Extracellular congophilic amyloid-beta senile neuritic plaques
Intracellular alpha-synuclein-positive cytoplasmic Lewy bodies
Intracellular spherical tau inclusions known as Pick bodies
Widespread cortical and striatal neuropil spongiform change
Intracytoplasmic rod-like eosinophilic Hirano actin bodies

explanation: Dementia with Lewy Bodies (DLB) is characterized by fluctuating cognition, recurrent detailed visual hallucinations, spontaneous parkinsonism, and early REM sleep behavior disorder. Neuropathology demonstrates round, eosinophilic intracytoplasmic Lewy bodies composed of aggregated alpha-synuclein in cortical and brainstem neurons.

stem: A 49-year-old woman makes inappropriate sexual comments, quits her job, compulsively shops, and hoards and gorges on candy. Memory is intact. Which pairing is correct?

options.text: Round argentophilic Pick inclusion bodies composed of hyperphosphorylated tau
Neocortical and nigral cytoplasmic Lewy bodies composed of alpha-synuclein
Paired helical filaments forming neurofibrillary tangles of insoluble tau
Widespread extracellular amyloid-beta plaques without associated pathology
Protease-resistant infectious prion protein scrapie isoform sheet fibrils

explanation: Behavioral variant frontotemporal lobar degeneration (bv-FTLD / Pick disease) presents in younger patients (50s-60s) with profound personality changes, social disinhibition, hyperorality, and apathy with relatively spared memory. Autopsy reveals prominent atrophy of the frontal and anterior temporal lobes with inclusions of hyperphosphorylated tau (Pick bodies) or TDP-43.

stem: A 63-year-old woman has rapid cognitive decline, gait ataxia, and myoclonus over weeks; MRI shows cortical ribboning. What is the pathogenic mechanism?

options.text: Alpha-helical cellular prion protein converts into beta-sheet scrapie isoform
Extracellular deposition of amyloid-beta peptides within cortical arterioles
Hyperphosphorylation and aggregation of microtubule-associated tau protein
Accumulation of misfolded alpha-synuclein within neuronal cytoplasmic inclusions
Depletion of nuclear TAR DNA-binding protein with aberrant cytoplasmic clumps

explanation: Creutzfeldt-Jakob Disease (CJD) is a rapidly progressive transmissible spongiform encephalopathy. Its pathogenesis involves the conformational conversion of normal alpha-helical cellular prion protein (PrPC) into the abnormal, protease-resistant beta-sheet scrapie isoform (PrPSc), which induces further template-directed misfolding.

stem: A 63-year-old woman presents with rapidly progressive cognitive decline, cerebellar gait ataxia, myoclonus, and cortical ribboning on diffusion-weighted MRI concerning for Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (CJD). Which diagnostic findings best support this diagnosis?

options.text: Marked mononuclear pleocytosis and low glucose on lumbar puncture testing
Periodic sharp waves on EEG, elevated 14-3-3 protein, and cortical ribboning
Intrathecal oligoclonal immunoglobulin bands on cerebrospinal electrophoresis
Selective bilateral hippocampal hyperintensity on fluid-attenuated sequences
Multiple ring-enhancing basal ganglia lesions with surrounding vasogenic edema

explanation: Diagnostic hallmarks of sporadic CJD include periodic synchronous sharp-wave complexes (PSWCs) on EEG, elevated 14-3-3 protein and positive real-time quaking-induced conversion (RT-QuIC) in the CSF, and cortical ribboning with basal ganglia hyperintensity on diffusion-weighted MRI (DWI).

stem: A 72-year-old man has a magnetic gait, urinary urgency, and memory loss. MRI shows ventriculomegaly out of proportion to sulcal atrophy. What is the best treatment?

options.text: Alzheimer disease neurodegeneration; oral acetylcholinesterase inhibitor
Subcortical vascular dementia; antiplatelet therapy and statin treatment
Parkinson disease dementia; carbidopa-levodopa dopaminergic replenishment
Idiopathic intracranial hypertension; oral acetazolamide diuretic therapy
Normal pressure hydrocephalus; large-volume tap test and VP shunt surgery

explanation: Normal Pressure Hydrocephalus (NPH) is characterized by the classic clinical triad of magnetic/apraxic gait ("wet, wacky, wobbly"), cognitive decline, and urinary incontinence. Neuroimaging shows ventriculomegaly disproportionate to sulcal enlargement. High-volume CSF removal via LP tap test is diagnostic, and placement of a ventriculoperitoneal (VP) shunt is curative.

stem: A 70-year-old man with hypertension and diabetes has stepwise cognitive decline with focal deficits after prior small strokes. MRI shows multiple infarcts. What best slows progression?

options.text: Creutzfeldt-Jakob prion disease; comfort care and palliative support
Behavioral frontotemporal dementia; selective serotonin reuptake drug
Advanced Alzheimer dementia; uncompetitive NMDA antagonist memantine
Vascular dementia; aggressive modification of systemic vascular risks
Lewy body dementia; acetylcholinesterase inhibitor patch rivastigmine

explanation: Vascular dementia is characterized by a stepwise cognitive decline temporally related to discrete cerebrovascular events (strokes) or progressive microvascular subcortical ischemic white matter disease. Management focuses on rigorous secondary prevention and control of vascular risk factors (hypertension, diabetes, lipids, smoking).

stem: A 40-year-old man has chorea, depression, and cognitive decline; MRI shows caudate atrophy. His father developed similar symptoms at age 50. What is the genetic basis?

options.text: Unstable CAG trinucleotide repeat expansion in HTT gene on chromosome 4
Unstable CTG trinucleotide repeat expansion in DMPK gene on chromosome 19
Unstable GAA trinucleotide repeat expansion in FXN gene on chromosome 9
Unstable CGG trinucleotide repeat expansion in FMR1 gene on X chromosome
Pathogenic missense mutation in presenilin-one gene on chromosome 14

explanation: Huntington disease is an autosomal dominant neurodegenerative disorder caused by an unstable CAG trinucleotide repeat expansion in the HTT gene on chromosome 4. It exhibits genetic anticipation (earlier onset and greater severity in successive generations, especially on paternal transmission). Striatal (caudate) atrophy is the pathological hallmark.

stem: A 50-year-old man with heavy alcohol use is found confused with bilateral horizontal nystagmus and a wide-based, unsteady gait. What is the best first step?

options.text: Immediate infusion of hypertonic dextrose solutions without other vitamins
Intravenous thiamine supplementation prior to or alongside dextrose fluids
High-dose intravenous folic acid and cyanocobalamin replacement therapy
Intravenous opioid antagonist naloxone administration for acute reversal
High-dose intravenous benzodiazepine lorazepam infusion for withdrawal

explanation: Wernicke encephalopathy is an acute neuropsychiatric syndrome caused by thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency, classically presenting with confusion, ophthalmoplegia/nystagmus, and ataxia. Administration of glucose without thiamine can precipitate or worsen encephalopathy because thiamine is a required cofactor for pyruvate dehydrogenase in glucose metabolism.

stem: Following an acute episode of Wernicke encephalopathy in a chronic alcohol user presenting with confusion, nystagmus, and ataxia, the patient develops persistent Korsakoff syndrome with severe anterograde amnesia and confabulation. Which anatomical structures are characteristically damaged?

options.text: Striatal caudate nucleus and bilateral putaminal lentiform nuclei
Mammillary bodies and anterior dorsomedial thalamic relay nuclei
Substantia nigra compacta and pontine locus coeruleus nuclei core
Amygdala nuclear complex and anterior parahippocampal uncal cortex
Cerebellar dentate nucleus and midbrain red nucleus tegmental core

explanation: Korsakoff syndrome is a chronic, largely irreversible amnestic-confabulatory state that follows untreated Wernicke encephalopathy. Neuropathology reveals petechial hemorrhages, gliosis, and atrophy of the mammillary bodies and anterior/dorsomedial nuclei of the thalamus.

stem: An 82-year-old man on hospital day 3 after hip fracture has fluctuating consciousness, inattention, disorganized speech, and visual hallucinations worse at night. What is the diagnosis?

options.text: Insidious onset with relentless progressive memory decline over years
Preserved attentional focus and sustained alertness throughout the day
Acute onset with fluctuating course and marked impairment in attention
Completely normal background electroencephalographic alpha rhythm trace
Permanent irreversible loss of functional independence without recovery

explanation: Delirium is an acute, fluctuating disturbance in attention, awareness, and cognition, typically triggered by underlying systemic medical illness (e.g., infection, metabolic derangement, medications, or postoperative state after fracture). Unlike dementia, delirium is characteristically fluctuating, features prominent inattention, and is reversible with treatment.

stem: A 25-year-old woman eating pizza feels a tightening sensation in her right arm that spreads to the hand and face. Next, her whole body stiffens and shakes for 2 minutes with urinary incontinence and bloody saliva, followed by 15 minutes of confusion. How is this seizure classified?

options.text: Generalized absence non-motor staring seizure event
Focal impaired-awareness sensory temporal lobe seizure
Primary generalized atonic sudden loss of tone seizure
Focal aware motor seizure evolving to bilateral convulsion
Primary generalized myoclonic juvenile-onset seizure jerk

explanation: A focal aware seizure starts in a circumscribed cortical area (e.g., motor cortex) with preserved consciousness and awareness. When motor activity progresses along the motor strip (Jacksonian march) and subsequently generalizes into a bilateral tonic-clonic convulsion with loss of consciousness, it is classified as a focal aware motor seizure evolving to bilateral tonic-clonic.

stem: A 7-year-old girl has daily 10-second staring spells with eyelid fluttering; she is unaware during them and recovers instantly. Hyperventilation reproduces an episode. Which EEG pattern is expected?

options.text: Continuous disorganized chaotic high-voltage hypsarrhythmia rhythm
Periodic synchronous sharp-wave complexes repeating once each second
Generalized symmetric three-hertz spike-and-slow-wave complexes
Focal anterior temporal sharp transients with phase reversal spikes
Frontal delta brush patterns with rhythmic beta frequency bursts

explanation: Absence seizures (petit mal) present in childhood with brief (5-10 second) staring spells, unresponsiveness, and minor automatisms (eyelid fluttering) without postictal confusion. The pathognomonic electroencephalogram (EEG) finding is symmetric, generalized 3-Hz spike-and-wave discharges triggered by hyperventilation.

stem: A 30-year-old man has been seizing continuously for 8 minutes in the emergency department. What is the first-line drug?

options.text: Intravenous phenytoin infusion administered as solitary initial drug
Intravenous levetiracetam bolus administered as solitary initial agent
Intravenous valproic acid loading dose administered without sedatives
Intravenous lorazepam followed promptly by non-sedating antiepileptic
Immediate continuous intravenous propofol infusion with intubation

explanation: Status epilepticus is defined as continuous seizure activity lasting >= 5 minutes or recurrent seizures without full recovery of consciousness. The first-line emergency medication is an IV benzodiazepine (lorazepam 4 mg IV or diazepam 10 mg IV; IM midazolam if no IV access), followed immediately by an IV non-sedating antiepileptic drug.

stem: Which feature favors a seizure over syncope?

options.text: Prompt immediate restitution of baseline clarity upon lying flat
Lateral border tongue lacerations and prolonged postictal stupor
Prominent autonomic prodrome with diaphoresis and lightheadness
Completely normal post-event serum prolactin levels in the blood
Complete absence of convulsive jerking or rhythmic limb twitches

explanation: Clinical features that strongly distinguish a generalized epileptic seizure from syncopal episodes include lateral tongue laceration (highly specific for generalized tonic-clonic seizures), prolonged postictal confusion/somnolence, elevated serum prolactin, and sustained rhythmic motor activity > 30 seconds.

stem: A 68-year-old man has a first generalized seizure. Which cause is most common in this age group?

options.text: Congenital focal cortical dysplasia developmental malformation
Mesial temporal hippocampal sclerosis from childhood febrile fits
Cerebrovascular disease including past stroke and ischemic changes
Perinatal hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy sustained during delivery
Inborn metabolic error such as adult-onset pyridoxine dependency

explanation: In adults aged 65 and older presenting with a first unprovoked seizure, cerebrovascular disease (including past ischemic stroke, intracerebral hemorrhage, and vascular white matter lesions) is the single most common identifiable underlying cause.

stem: A 16-year-old girl has morning jerks of the arms that make her drop objects, and a generalized tonic-clonic seizure after a night of sleep deprivation. EEG shows 4–6 Hz polyspike-and-wave. What is the diagnosis?

options.text: Carbamazepine sodium channel blocker
Phenytoin hydantoin class anticonvulsant
Valproic acid broad-spectrum antiepileptic
Ethosuximide selective succinimide agent
Gabapentin calcium channel alpha-two ligand

explanation: Juvenile Myoclonic Epilepsy (JME / Janz syndrome) characteristically presents in adolescence with bilateral morning myoclonic jerks of the upper limbs, typically triggered by sleep deprivation or alcohol. Valproic acid is the first-line antiepileptic of choice due to its broad-spectrum efficacy against myoclonic, absence, and generalized tonic-clonic seizures.

stem: A 6-year-old boy has sudden brief loss of muscle tone causing head drops and falls, without convulsive movements. What is the seizure type?

options.text: Extensive cortical neuropil spongiform vacuolation and loss
Hippocampal pyramidal cell loss with marked dense gliosis
Perivenular oligodendrocyte demyelination with foam cells
Microglial nodules surrounding viral inclusions in neurons
Abundant neurofibrillary tangles formed of insoluble tau

explanation: Atonic seizures ("drop attacks") are characterized by a sudden, brief (<2 seconds) complete loss of postural muscle tone, causing the patient to collapse to the ground or experience sudden head drops, often resulting in traumatic facial injuries. They are typically seen in severe childhood epileptic encephalopathies such as Lennox-Gastaut syndrome.

stem: A 24-year-old woman has a second unprovoked generalized tonic-clonic seizure in 6 months. Examination, labs, CT, and EEG are normal. What is the best management?

options.text: Potential exacerbation of absence and myoclonic seizure activity
High risk of precipitating acute necrotizing hemorrhagic pancreatitis
Induction of life-threatening severe hypertensive vascular crisis
Complete irreversible shutdown of hepatic cytochrome P450 oxidation
Marked reduction of renal tubular reabsorption of urinary calcium

explanation: Following a second unprovoked seizure occurring > 24 hours after the first, the patient meets diagnostic criteria for epilepsy, and the recurrence risk over the subsequent 5 years exceeds 60-80%. Long-term antiepileptic monotherapy is indicated to prevent future recurrent seizures.

stem: A 28-year-old woman has a rising epigastric sensation and déjà vu, then stares and lip-smacks for 90 seconds, followed by confusion. MRI shows hippocampal sclerosis. What is the seizure type?

options.text: Progression into medically refractory epileptic encephalopathy
Severe cumulative cognitive decline and status epilepticus
Spontaneous remission by adolescence with normal cognition
Obligate requirement for aggressive combination anticonvulsants
Rapid progressive neurodegeneration and loss of motor skills

explanation: Focal impaired awareness seizures arising from the mesial temporal lobe typically begin with an epigastric rising sensation, déjà vu, or olfactory aura, followed by vacant staring, unresponsiveness, oral automatisms (chewing, lip smacking), and manual automatisms (fumbling with clothes), followed by postictal confusion and amnesia.

stem: An 18-month-old has a 3-minute generalized tonic-clonic seizure with a temperature of 39.8°C, then returns to baseline; the neurologic exam is normal. What is the best management?

options.text: Carbamazepine sodium channel blocker
Phenytoin hydantoin class anticonvulsant
Adrenocorticotropic hormone or vigabatrin
Ethosuximide selective succinimide agent
Lorazepam parenteral short-acting sedative

explanation: A simple febrile seizure is defined as a generalized seizure lasting < 15 minutes that occurs in a neurologically normal child aged 6 months to 5 years in the setting of fever, without recurrence in 24 hours. Simple febrile seizures carry an excellent prognosis with no increased risk of intellectual disability; management consists of parental reassurance and antipyretics.

stem: A 32-year-old man has mesial temporal lobe seizures that persist despite adequate trials of two antiseizure drugs; MRI shows hippocampal sclerosis. What is the next step?

options.text: Increased frequency of chloride channel opening events
Increased duration of individual chloride channel openings
Use-dependent blockade of neuronal voltage-gated sodium
Selective inhibition of low-threshold T-type calcium channels
Inhibition of presynaptic GABA reuptake transporter pumps

explanation: Mesial temporal sclerosis (hippocampal sclerosis) is the most common identifiable pathology in adult drug-resistant temporal lobe epilepsy. Magnetic resonance imaging demonstrates unilateral hippocampal atrophy with increased T2/FLAIR signal intensity, reflecting pyramidal neuronal loss and dense fibrillary astrogliosis.

stem: A man in status epilepticus receives IV lorazepam. What is its mechanism of action?

options.text: Increased frequency of chloride channel opening bursts
Increased duration of individual chloride channel openings
Selective blockade of low-voltage T-type calcium pores
Targeted inhibition of mitochondrial GABA transaminase enzyme
Irreversible covalent blockade of synaptic NMDA glutamate

explanation: Benzodiazepines (lorazepam, diazepam, midazolam) bind allosterically to GABAA receptors and enhance the action of GABA by increasing the FREQUENCY of chloride channel opening, leading to membrane hyperpolarization and rapid suppression of epileptiform activity.

stem: A patient given a benzodiazepine for seizures also drinks alcohol. Which adverse effect is of greatest concern?

options.text: Fibrous gingival hyperplasia and excess facial hirsutism
Profound agranulocytosis and idiosyncratic aplastic anemia
Severe acute necrotizing pancreatitis with elevated lipase
Profound central respiratory depression and hypoventilation
Extensive epidermal necrolysis with full-thickness mucosal loss

explanation: Both benzodiazepines and ethanol act as central nervous system depressants by potentiating GABAA receptor chloride currents. Concurrent ingestion produces synergistic, supra-additive sedation that can precipitate fatal respiratory depression and coma.

stem: A 28-year-old woman with focal seizures is started on carbamazepine. What is its mechanism of action?

options.text: Allosteric enhancement of GABA-A chloride opening frequency
Selective inhibition of thalamic T-type calcium channel pores
Irreversible inhibition of mitochondrial GABA transaminase enzyme
Allosteric prolongation of GABA-A chloride pore open state time
Use-dependent block of voltage-gated sodium channel inactivation

explanation: Carbamazepine is a first-line agent for focal seizures. Its mechanism of action involves use-dependent / frequency-dependent blockade of voltage-gated neuronal sodium channels, preferentially binding to and prolonging the inactivated state to suppress high-frequency repetitive action potential firing.

stem: A 45-year-old woman on carbamazepine develops fever and sore throat; the absolute neutrophil count is near zero. Which adverse effect is this?

options.text: Megaloblastic anemia secondary to accelerated folate metabolism
Immune thrombocytopenia driven by antiplatelet autoantibodies
Profound agranulocytosis with associated risk of aplastic anemia
Autoimmune Coombs-positive hemolytic anemia with spherocytosis
Secondary polycythemia caused by autonomous marrow proliferation

explanation: Carbamazepine carries a black-box warning for severe bone marrow suppression, specifically agranulocytosis (severe absolute neutropenia) and aplastic anemia. Baseline and periodic complete blood count (CBC) monitoring is recommended.

stem: A 70-year-old woman on carbamazepine is confused; sodium is 121 mEq/L, she is euvolemic, and urine osmolality is 450 mOsm/kg. What explains this?

options.text: Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone release
Central neurogenic diabetes insipidus vasopressin deficit
Primary adrenal insufficiency with mineralocorticoid loss
Psychogenic primary polydipsia with compulsive water drinking
Cerebral salt wasting syndrome with hypovolemic natriuresis

explanation: Carbamazepine can induce syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH), especially in older adults. It enhances renal collecting duct sensitivity to circulating ADH, producing euvolemic hyponatremia with inappropriately concentrated urine.

stem: What is the mechanism of action of valproic acid?

options.text: Selective allosteric enhancement of GABA-A chloride opening frequency
Selective blockade of low-threshold thalamic T-type calcium channels
Selective use-dependent blockade of voltage-gated sodium channels only
Blockade of sodium and calcium channels plus inhibition of GABA breakdown
Selective allosteric prolongation of GABA-A channel opening duration

explanation: Valproic acid has a broad mechanism of action: it blocks voltage-gated sodium channels, blocks low-threshold T-type calcium channels in the thalamus, and increases inhibitory GABA transmission by inhibiting GABA transaminase and stimulating glutamate decarboxylase.

stem: A patient on valproic acid develops jaundice with markedly elevated AST and ALT; another develops severe epigastric pain with elevated lipase. Which adverse effects does this illustrate?

options.text: Fibrous gingival hyperplasia and androgen-independent coarsening hirsutism
Profound agranulocytosis and idiosyncratic irreversible aplastic anemia
Stevens-Johnson syndrome and widespread toxic epidermal detachment slough
Central respiratory depression and rapid development of physiological habit
Fulminant idiosyncratic hepatotoxicity and acute necrotizing pancreatitis

explanation: Valproic acid carries black-box warnings for idiosyncratic fulminant hepatotoxicity (most common in children < 2 years and patients with underlying mitochondrial disorders) and acute necrotizing pancreatitis, which can develop rapidly regardless of treatment duration.

stem: A woman with generalized epilepsy plans a pregnancy. Which drug carries the greatest risk of neural tube defects?

options.text: Lamotrigine phenyltriazine anticonvulsant
Ethosuximide selective succinimide agent
Valproic acid broad-spectrum antiepileptic
Lorazepam intermediate-acting benzodiazepine
Phenytoin hydantoin class sodium antagonist

explanation: Valproic acid is the most teratogenic antiepileptic drug, carrying a 1-2% risk of neural tube defects (spina bifida, anencephaly) due to folate metabolism interference, as well as significant risks of major congenital malformations and impaired cognitive development; it is avoided in women of childbearing potential.

stem: What is the mechanism of action of phenytoin?

options.text: Use-dependent blockade of neuronal voltage-gated sodium channels
Allosteric enhancement of GABA-A chloride pore opening frequency
Selective blockade of low-threshold thalamic T-type calcium pores
Irreversible inhibition of mitochondrial GABA transaminase enzymes
Direct pharmacological opening of inward-rectifying potassium pores

explanation: Phenytoin suppresses focal and generalized tonic-clonic seizures by use-dependent blockade of voltage-gated neuronal sodium channels, binding selectively to the inactivated conformation to prevent repetitive sustained axonal firing.

stem: A 30-year-old man on phenytoin for 2 years has gum overgrowth, coarse facial features, and excess hair growth. Which adverse effects are these?

options.text: Fulminant hepatic necrosis and microvesicular steatosis
Fibrous gingival hyperplasia and androgenic hirsutism
Acute necrotizing pancreatitis with elevated amylase
Lumbosacral myelomeningocele neural tube birth defects
Profound euvolemic hyponatremia from inappropriate ADH

explanation: Chronic phenytoin therapy is characteristically associated with gingival hyperplasia (induced by PDGF-stimulated gingival fibroblast proliferation) and hirsutism. Other chronic side effects include coarsening of facial features, peripheral neuropathy, and megaloblastic anemia due to folate malabsorption.

stem: A 35-year-old man stable on phenytoin has a modest dose increase and develops nystagmus, ataxia, and diplopia; the serum level is far higher than expected. Why?

options.text: Potent autoinduction of hepatic cytochrome P450 enzymes
Linear first-order clearance with accelerated absorption
Displacement from circulating serum albumin proteins only
Significant reduction of active renal tubular clearance
Saturation of hepatic clearance yielding zero-order kinetics

explanation: Phenytoin exhibits nonlinear, saturable (Michaelis-Menten / zero-order) elimination kinetics within the therapeutic range. Once hepatic metabolizing enzymes (CYP2C9) are saturated, small incremental dosage increases lead to disproportionately large elevations in serum drug levels, precipitating acute neurotoxicity (nystagmus, ataxia, diplopia).

stem: A 24-year-old woman taking an oral contraceptive is prescribed phenytoin. What interaction should be anticipated?

options.text: Competitive CYP450 inhibition elevating serum estrogen levels
Impaired gastrointestinal absorption of circulating estrogen pills
Enhanced renal tubular reabsorption of circulating progestins
Potent CYP450 induction accelerating contraceptive clearance
Absence of pharmacokinetic or pharmacodynamic drug interactions

explanation: Phenytoin is a potent inducer of hepatic cytochrome P450 enzymes (particularly CYP3A4). It significantly accelerates the metabolic clearance of estrogen and progestin components of oral contraceptives, leading to subtherapeutic hormone levels and contraceptive failure.

stem: What is the mechanism of action of lamotrigine?

options.text: Blockade of low-threshold T-type calcium channels in thalamic neurons
Blockade of voltage-gated sodium channels and reduced glutamate release
Allosteric modulation increasing frequency of chloride channel opening
Irreversible inhibition of mitochondrial GABA transaminase catabolism
Allosteric modulation increasing duration of chloride channel openings

explanation: Lamotrigine suppresses seizures by blocking voltage-gated neuronal sodium channels and stabilizing presynaptic neuronal membranes, which inhibits the downstream vesicular release of excitatory amino acid neurotransmitters (glutamate and aspartate).

stem: A 20-year-old woman 2 weeks into rapid lamotrigine titration develops fever and a painful rash with mucosal erosions and epidermal detachment. What is the adverse effect?

options.text: Fibrous gingival hyperplasia and androgenic facial hirsutism
Fulminant idiosyncratic hepatitis with raised transaminases
Profound idiosyncratic agranulocytosis and bone marrow aplasia
Symmetrical length-dependent sensorimotor axonal neuropathy
Stevens-Johnson syndrome or toxic epidermal necrolysis reaction

explanation: Lamotrigine carries a black-box warning for severe cutaneous adverse reactions, including Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS) and toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN). The risk is strongly correlated with rapid initial dose titration and concurrent use of valproic acid (which inhibits lamotrigine glucuronidation).

stem: An 8-year-old with absence seizures is treated with ethosuximide. What is its mechanism of action?

options.text: Use-dependent blockade of neuronal voltage-gated sodium channels
Blockade of low-threshold T-type calcium channels in thalamus
Allosteric enhancement of GABA-A chloride opening frequency
Inhibition of mitochondrial GABA transaminase catabolic enzyme
Competitive antagonism of ionotropic NMDA glutamate receptors

explanation: Ethosuximide is the drug of choice for absence seizures. It acts selectively by blocking low-threshold T-type voltage-gated calcium channels in thalamic relay neurons, thereby disrupting the pacemaker current responsible for generating the synchronous 3-Hz spike-and-wave discharge.

stem: Which drug and adverse effect pairing is correct?

options.text: Lamotrigine therapy paired with severe fibrous gingival hyperplasia
Phenytoin treatment paired with idiosyncratic acute agranulocytosis
Valproic acid paired with acute pancreatitis and hepatotoxicity
Carbamazepine paired with fibrous gingival hyperplasia and overgrowth
Lorazepam therapy paired with idiosyncratic toxic liver necrosis

explanation: Valproic acid is correctly paired with acute pancreatitis and hepatotoxicity. Phenytoin causes gingival hyperplasia and hirsutism (not agranulocytosis); carbamazepine causes agranulocytosis, aplastic anemia, and SIADH (not gingival hyperplasia); lamotrigine causes Stevens-Johnson syndrome.
